hints: Start by thinking about what makes meiosis different from mitosis in how chromosomes are handled.
Recall what happens when homologous chromosomes pair up together in prophase I.
Think about which chromatids touch and what is physically swapped between them.
Consider why swapping sections of DNA creates new allele combinations and breaks linkage groups.
Move to metaphase I and picture how the pairs line up at the equator - is the orientation fixed?
Remember there is a second division too - think about how chromatids separate in meiosis II.
Now leave meiosis and think about fertilisation - how many possible sperm and eggs could fuse?
Pull it together to explain why no two offspring get exactly the same combination of alleles.
walkthrough:
Crossing Over Creates New Chromatids**
In prophase I homologous chromosomes pair to form a bivalent. Non-sister chromatids touch at points called chiasmata and swap exactly corresponding sections. This is crossing over. Because DNA is exchanged, alleles that were on the same parental chromosome are now mixed together.

Why This Matters for Variation**
Genes on the same chromosome are normally inherited together as a linkage group. Crossing over breaks this link and makes a recombinant chromatid with a new combination of alleles. Every crossover event is in a different place, so the four chromatids in each bivalent end up genetically different.

Independent Assortment Shuffles Whole Chromosomes**
In metaphase I the bivalents line up at the equator. Whether the maternal or paternal homologue of each pair faces a given pole is completely random and independent of the other pairs. In humans with 23 pairs this alone gives over 8 million possible gamete chromosome combinations. A further independent assortment of sister chromatids occurs in metaphase II.

Fertilisation Multiplies the Variation**
Meiosis produces haploid gametes that are all genetically different. At fertilisation any one sperm can fuse with any one egg at random. Random mating in the population adds even more mixing. Together crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation ensure offspring are genetically unique.

Final answer: In prophase I, crossing over / formation of chiasmata occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes / bivalent, with exchange of DNA. This breaks linkage groups and produces new combinations of alleles. In metaphase I, independent / random assortment of homologous chromosomes / bivalents at the equator occurs, with independent assortment of chromatids / chromosomes in metaphase II. Random mating and random fusion / fertilisation of gametes produces further variation.

hints: Start by recalling the parts of an operon - structural genes plus control regions.
Think about the extra gene outside the operon that controls it and what protein it makes all the time.
Picture where that control protein sits on the DNA when lactose is absent.
Consider what that binding does to RNA polymerase and transcription.
Now add lactose - think about what small molecule binds to what protein.
Think about how binding lactose changes the shape of the control protein.
Link the release of the control region to switching transcription and enzyme synthesis on or off.
walkthrough:
The Parts of the System**
The lac operon contains structural genes for lactose-metabolising enzymes plus a promoter where RNA polymerase binds and an operator switch next to it. Outside the operon a regulatory gene is always making a protein called the repressor.

Switched Off Without Lactose**
When lactose is absent, the repressor protein has the right shape to sit firmly on the operator DNA. Sitting there it physically blocks the promoter. RNA polymerase cannot bind, so the structural genes cannot be transcribed into mRNA and no enzymes like beta-galactosidase are made. This saves energy.

Switched On With Lactose**
When lactose is present, lactose / allolactose acts as an inducer and binds to the repressor protein. The repressor changes shape so it no longer fits the operator and falls off. The promoter is now free.

Transcription and Enzyme Production**
RNA polymerase can now bind to the promoter and transcribe the structural genes into mRNA, which is translated into the lactose-digesting enzymes. When lactose runs out, free repressor binds the operator again and the system switches off.

Final answer: Regulatory gene codes for repressor protein which binds to operator. In absence of lactose, repressor blocks promoter, RNA polymerase cannot bind, structural genes not transcribed, no mRNA and no enzymes synthesised. In presence of lactose, lactose / allolactose binds to repressor, repressor changes shape and no longer binds / leaves operator, promoter unblocked, RNA polymerase binds, genes transcribed / switched on and enzymes synthesised.
